items.prompt: Priya reads the 7-times table five times Monday night. Per this unit, has she reached "understanding" of the table by the end of that fifth read?
choices: Yes — five careful rereads automatically converts into understanding, since repetition alone is what builds the skill
Not necessarily — rereading is exposure; understanding means being able to produce or apply the material unaided, which the reading itself never tested
No — nothing short of several more weeks of daily study sessions could possibly count as real understanding here
It depends only on the raw number of times she reread the page, regardless of whether anything was ever tested afterward
items.explanation: Exposure (reading, watching) and understanding (producing it unaided, applying it, predicting under new conditions) are different things. Rereading can make the material feel familiar without ever testing whether it's retrievable — which is exactly what Wednesday's cold quiz revealed.

items.prompt: Why did Priya's fifth read of the 7-times table feel smoother and more confident than her first read, even though nothing was actually tested in between?
choices: Because the 7-times table itself objectively became a simpler, easier topic each additional time she read through it
Because processing something already seen gets easier with repetition (perceptual fluency), and that ease gets misread as a sign of deeper understanding rather than just familiarity with the page
Because she was unconsciously memorizing the correct answers without ever noticing she was doing so at all
There's no real reason behind it — the smoothness she felt was essentially random and unrelated to the rereading
items.explanation: The fluency illusion is the mismatch between processing ease (which genuinely increases with repeated exposure) and retrievability (the ability to reproduce the material unaided), which doesn't automatically increase just because the page reads more smoothly.

✨ Processing feels easier (real)
↓
⚠️ Misread as "I understand it better"

Why: ease of processing and ability to retrieve are two different things — only one of them was ever tested by rereading.

items.prompt: Per this unit, what makes active recall (getting quizzed cold) a more honest signal than passive exposure (rereading), even though rereading is lower-effort?
choices: Active recall is more honest mainly because it simply takes longer to complete than a quick reread does
Active recall either works or visibly doesn't — it produces a real result instead of just a feeling, while rereading only ever produces a feeling of increasing familiarity
Passive exposure is actually just as honest a signal as active recall — this unit just happens to prefer the other one
Active recall is only a more honest signal when it's done inside a formal classroom setting with a teacher present
items.explanation: The key difference isn't effort for its own sake — it's that active recall produces an outcome that can be checked (got it right or didn't), while passive exposure only ever produces a subjective sense of ease that was never actually checked against anything.
items.reference:
Passive exposureFeels smoother each time — never checked
Active recallEither produces the answer or doesn't — checked

Why: a signal that's never checked against anything can't be honest or dishonest — it's just a feeling.

Low effort isn't inherently bad, and high effort isn't inherently good — the point is which one produces a signal that can actually be wrong, and therefore actually informative.

items.explanation: Rereading never confronts you with a wrong answer — there's nothing to get wrong. Active recall does, which is exactly why it's more informative and also why it feels worse: the discomfort comes from actually encountering the gap instead of gliding past it.

items.prompt: Per this unit, is the point to avoid rereading or watching tutorials altogether?
choices: Yes — passive exposure like reading or watching should be avoided entirely in favor of recall from the very start
No — exposure is a necessary first step; the point is to not stop there, and to force a retrieval step afterward instead of mistaking the exposure itself for the finish line
Yes, but only for topics that involve purely memorized facts like multiplication tables, not conceptual material
No — the two methods are equally effective at building understanding and it doesn't matter which one is used
items.explanation: This unit explicitly isn't an argument against reading or exposure — you can't understand what you've never encountered. Priya still had to read the table before she could do anything with it; the discipline is adding a retrieval step afterward, not skipping exposure.
items.reference:
① Get exposed to the material
② Close the source
③ Try to reproduce or apply it, unaided

Why: exposure is necessary but not sufficient — the retrieval step is what's usually missing, not the exposure itself.
items.learnMore:

items.prompt: Per L2, what exactly is "perceptual fluency," and is it a real phenomenon or a made-up one?

It only ever applies to visual material like diagrams or charts, and never applies to plain written text

items.explanation: Perceptual fluency is a real, measurable increase in processing speed/ease with repeated exposure. L2 is careful to say the feeling it produces is genuine — the mistake is using that real feeling as evidence for a different, unmeasured claim (retrievability).

items.prompt: Per L2, why is "recognizing 56 as the right answer next to '7×8'" a weaker skill than "producing 56 with nothing printed at all"?

items.prompt: Per L2, what are the two specific "tells" to scan for in a Feynman-style unaided explanation?
choices: How long the spoken explanation takes to deliver, and roughly how many distinct words it ends up using
A term used without ever explaining what it actually means, and any point where the explanation resorts to something like "I just know it" or "it's automatic"
Whether the explanation was written down on paper or instead spoken out loud to another person

items.explanation: L2 names two specific tells: jargon standing in for a mechanism (a term used but never unpacked), and a stall where the explanation can't go further except by asserting fluency ("I just know it"). Both mark exactly where retrieval ran out.

① A term used but never actually explained
② A stall — "I just know it," "it's automatic"

Why: both tells mark the exact point retrieval ran out, which is more useful than a vague sense the explanation "wasn't great."

items.prompt: Why does the Feynman technique require explaining with "no looking at the source," rather than allowing a quick glance back if needed?
choices: Looking back at the source is actually fine — the no-peeking rule is really just an arbitrary tradition

Allowing a glance back would let recognition (matching what's on the page) substitute for retrieval (producing it from memory) at exactly the moment that matters, defeating the whole point of the test
The source material is usually unavailable in real study situations anyway, so this rule changes nothing practical
It's only enforced as a rule for advanced learners, and doesn't apply to beginners just starting out
items.explanation: The entire diagnostic value of the technique depends on testing retrieval, not recognition. A glance back at the source at a hard moment would let recognition quietly do the work retrieval was supposed to do, hiding exactly the gap the technique is meant to surface.
